analysis.one_liner: Cuts brand-name biologic drug market exclusivity from 12 years to 7 years, speeding cheaper competing versions.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to shorten biologic drug exclusivity from 12 to 7 years was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs—complex medicines made from living cells, used for conditions like arthritis, cancer, and diabetes—currently get 12 years of protection from cheaper competing copies called biosimilars. The PRICED Act would cut that protection to 7 years, so cheaper versions could reach the market sooner and prices would fall earlier. The change would apply only to drugs approved after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take biologic drugs, including millions treated for autoimmune diseases, cancer, and diabetes, would gain access to lower-priced biosimilar copies years earlier. Insurers and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid would also see drug costs fall. Biosimilar manufacturers would gain a larger market sooner.

how_it_helps.text: The bill shortens the exclusivity period for brand-name biological products from 12 years to 7 years, amending the Public Health Service Act by striking '12 years' and inserting '7 years'.
Under the shortened period, biosimilar copies could be marketed seven years after the reference brand-name product is licensed, instead of the current twelve.
The change applies only to biological products licensed by the FDA on or after enactment, so it does not disturb existing monopoly periods.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers would lose five years of monopoly pricing on newly approved drugs, an extended window of high-revenue sales that currently funds much of the industry's returns.

drawbacks.text: Brand manufacturers and some policy analysts argue that the 12-year exclusivity period exists to recoup the large development costs and clinical testing that biologics require, and that a shorter period could weaken incentives to invest in new biological medicines.
Because the change applies only to drugs approved after enactment, patients would see no price relief on existing biologics for years, since their 12-year exclusivity windows remain untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: earlier competition means lower prices for patients and payers, while drugmakers earn less on each new biologic and might invest somewhat less in research. The strongest honest criticism is not that the goal is wrong but that the bill's prospective-only design delays any benefit for years, and the bill died before that trade-off could ever be debated or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the PRICED Act in the Senate on June 23, 2016, joined by Sen. John McCain as cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on June 23, 2016.
No further action—no hearing, markup, floor vote, or House companion action—is recorded; the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drugmakers are better off, because they keep the full 12-year exclusivity period and the years of monopoly-priced sales that come with it. Patients continue paying brand-name prices for these drugs.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut biologic exclusivity from 12 to 7 years.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred—no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the remaining months of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Republican cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; the record shows only that the referral committee, chaired by a Republican, took no action.

industries.note: The bill would cut five years from the 12-year monopoly window during which these companies can sell newly approved biologics without cheaper competition, a period that supports some of the industry's highest margins. Keeping the current 12-year rule means patients and government programs keep paying monopoly prices longer.
A shorter exclusivity period would let biosimilar companies enter the market for each new biologic five years sooner, expanding their business while lowering prices for patients.
